newsitem.title: FRANCE: Boeing, Airbus fly into airshow dogfight.
newsitem.headline: Boeing, Airbus fly into airshow dogfight.

text.p: The world's leading airliner manufacturers, Boeing Co and Airbus Industrie, traded insults and veiled threats in a trans-Atlantic dogfight at the Paris air show on Sunday.
Airbus managing director Jean Pierson accused Boeing of trying to kill off the competition. Boeing's commercial aircraft head, Ron Woodard, spat back that Pierson had "slipped a cog".
"He's got totally paranoid and we're not listening to what he says because he is flailing around," Woodard told reporters.

The industry is thriving but the U.S. aerospace and defence industries are consolidating rapidly. Boeing's plan to take over U.S. rival McDonnell Douglas has unnerved its fragmented European rivals who say Boeing is already too big and threatens to drive them out of the market.
Pierson made his charges in a signed article published in French daily Le Monde and distributed to reporters at the air show.

He said McDonnell Douglas, anticipating a deal with Boeing, deliberately failed in the competition to develop a new Joint Strike Fighter for the U.S. military and also scrapped plans for an MDXX super-jumbo airliner.

"These two decisions... anticipated any eventual objections of the American anti-trust authorities over the reduction of competition in these two sectors following a merger with Boeing," Pierson wrote.
"It's total lunacy," Woodard told reporters. "Those remarks should be withdrawn...We're not into conspiracy theories."

Boeing is battling to convince the European Commission that there was nothing anti-competitive about its $14 billion dollar deal with McDonnell Douglas, which it says accounts for only four percent of new aircraft sales last year.
Boeing is hoping for a favourable ruling by July 1 from the U.S. Federal Trade Commission, but that could leave Europe at odds with Washington and raise the prospect of a trade war.
"I am sure the merger is going to get approved," Woodard said. "If things did get into some sort of trade friction there would be people getting hurt on both sides of the Atlantic."
He said the Franco-U.S. made CFM56 engines which power Boeing's biggest selling aircraft, the 737, under exclusive contract, was one example of European companies benefiting from Boeing's business.

State-owned Snecma, the French partner with General Electric Co, on the CFM56 engine was expected to gain $6.8 billion in sales over the next five years, having netted $2.5 billion from previous 737 sales.
The engine programme supports 11,000 French jobs, Woodard said. "No-one in Europe has ever objected to this exclusive contract," he said.

But Woodard also warned that Boeing was pushing ahead with a billion dollar investment to overhaul production and expected to be building planes next year in an average of six months each -- half of the best that Airbus hopes to achieve.
"Anyone having a difficult time competing with us now is going to have a horrible time with the new system," he said. "This is going to bury them."

Another European gripe is over Boeing's recent series of 20-year exclusive sales deals with three U.S. carriers American Airlines. Delta Air Lines and Continental which are planning to renew their entire fleets.
Pierson said that because planes have a 25-year life, an exclusive agreement for 20 years can annihilate competition. "It is for eternity. It is not for 20 years, that is the problem," he said.
